scenes.spec: hand pulling the coolant reservoir cap area into view, low tank against the MIN line
scenes.narration: Every few weeks, the same ritual: the low-coolant light blinks on, you top up the tank, and everything's fine again. For a while. And each time, a little voice asks — *where is it going?* Here's the uncomfortable rule from last episode, worth repeating because it drives this entire hour: **coolant does not evaporate.** The system is sealed. A dropping level is coolant leaving — into your driveway, into another part of the car, or out the tailpipe as steam. Tonight we find which, with a flashlight, a piece of cardboard, and about ten minutes of actual effort.

scenes.spec: channel card — "Why Is My Car Doing That?"
three-way split — "Puddle you can see" / "Level drops, no puddle" / "Smell or fog inside the car"
scenes.narration: Three versions of this problem, three different hunts. **There's a puddle.** Congratulations — external leak, the easy hunt. Coolant is dyed (green, orange, pink, blue) and smells faintly sweet. Clear odorless water near the front passenger area on a hot day is usually AC condensation — that one's normal and free. **Level drops, no puddle, ever.** The sneaky tier: coolant leaving somewhere you can't see — while driving, onto hot parts that flash it to steam, or *inside* the engine. That's where the pressure test and the previous two episodes come in. **You smell it inside the car** — sweet smell from the vents, an oily film fogging the windshield, damp passenger-side carpet: that's the heater core, the radiator's little cousin living inside your dash.

scenes.section: THE CARDBOARD TEST — FREE DIAGNOSIS OVERNIGHT
scenes.spec: car parked over a large flattened cardboard box overnight; morning: drip stains mapped to zones — front/center/rear of engine bay
scenes.narration: Before any shop visit: park overnight over a big flattened cardboard box. Morning gives you a map — WHAT color landed WHERE. Coolant color at the very front: radiator territory. Mid-engine, driver or passenger side: hoses or water pump. A stain that's engine-oil brown is a different episode. No stains at all plus a dropping level: internal or under-pressure-only leak — skip straight to the pressure-test section. Bring the cardboard story (or a photo) to your shop and you've cut real diagnostic time. [TECH CONFIRM — do customers who bring driveway-map info actually save diag money at FHT, or does the shop redo it anyway?]

scenes.section: LEAK SITE #1 — HOSES AND CLAMPS (most common)
scenes.spec: cooling loop from ep 5 — hose runs highlighted; closeup on a hose end swollen and seeping at the clamp
scenes.narration: Rubber lives a hard life next to an engine: heat cycles, pressure cycles, ozone. Hoses fail at the ends first — swelling, hairline splits, seepage at clamps that leaves crusty dried-coolant trails (white, green, or rusty residue you can spot with a flashlight). Squeeze test on a COLD engine: a healthy hose is firm and springy; a dying one is either rock-hard and crackly or soft and mushy. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the squeeze-test description; anything you check that beginners can too?]

scenes.spec: radiator — plastic end tanks, crimp seams, fin-field; seep points glowing at tank seams
scenes.narration: Modern radiators are aluminum cores with **plastic end tanks** crimped on — and those tanks and crimp seams are where age shows: hairline cracks, seep-then-split behavior, crusty residue trails. Road debris punctures happen too. Small radiator leaks love to seal themselves with grime for weeks, then let go on a road trip. [TECH CONFIRM — plastic end-tank cracking: fair to call it THE radiator failure mode you see?]

scenes.section: LEAK SITE #3 — WATER PUMP WEEP HOLE
scenes.spec: pump from ep 5 — weep hole underneath, slow drip, dried trail down the block
scenes.narration: Last episode's tell-tale, now in the hunt: pumps announce their seal is dying through a designed **weep hole**. The drip often only runs when the engine's hot and pressurized — so the cardboard catches it but your casual glance doesn't. Dried streaks running DOWN from the pump area are the fingerprint. A weeping pump is a *scheduled* replacement, not an emergency — but scheduled means soon. [TECH CONFIRM — your typical weep-to-failure runway estimate]

scenes.section: LEAK SITE #4 — THE HEATER CORE (the one inside the car)
scenes.spec: dash cross-section — heater core behind the dashboard, sweet fog path to windshield, drip path to passenger carpet
scenes.narration: The heater core is a small radiator inside the dash. When it leaks, the evidence is interior: sweet smell from the vents, oily film on the inside of the windshield that keeps coming back, damp or sweet-smelling passenger-front carpet. This is the leak people chase under the hood for months while it's been raining inside the dashboard. Repair honesty: the part is cheap and the labor is famous — on many cars the whole dash comes out. [TECH CONFIRM — dash-out labor hours range you quote; any cars where it's easy?]

scenes.section: LEAK SITE #5 — INTERNAL: THE PRESSURE TEST TIER
scenes.spec: pressure tester pumping the system; gauge holding vs falling; cutaway showing coolant seeping into a cylinder
scenes.narration: No puddle anywhere, cardboard's clean, level keeps dropping: the coolant is leaving *inside*. A shop **pressure test** pumps the cooled system to operating pressure and watches the gauge: holds = look again outside under pressure; falls with nothing visible = internal path. From there it's the white-smoke episode's territory — block test, combustion gases in the coolant, head gasket conversation. The good news: the test itself is quick and cheap compared to what it rules in or out. [TECH CONFIRM — pressure test + block test pricing at FHT for section ranges below]

scenes.section: THE REPAIR — WHAT THE MONEY LOOKS LIKE
scenes.spec: decision tree — leak site in, job out
scenes.narration: Ranked by wallet impact, roughly: a hose is parts-cheap and quick; a radiator is a mid-size job; a pump varies wildly by engine (some are front-and-center, some live behind the timing cover and the labor IS the job); the heater core is cheap-part-heavy-labor; internal leaks are last episode's head-gasket math. [callout: typical US shop ranges — "Hose: $___–$___ · Radiator: $___–$___ · Water pump: $___–$___ · Heater core: $___–$___ · Pressure test: $___–$___"] [TECH CONFIRM — fill from real FHT invoices; pump range may want a "timing-cover engines cost more" footnote] One more honesty beat: **stop-leak products.** The bottles that promise to seal it from the inside. Emergency-limp-home tool at best; at worst they clog the heater core and radiator you were trying to save. [TECH CONFIRM — your actual stance on stop-leak, including any cleanup jobs it's caused in your bays — this is a trust-building beat]

scenes.spec: three-tier verdict card — "Monitor weekly" / "This week" / "Stop driving"
scenes.narration: **Monitor weekly:** level dropped once, no repeat, no smell, no stains. Mark the tank, watch it. Systems do burp air pockets after service. **This week:** any *repeating* drop, any stain on the cardboard, sweet smell anywhere, weep trails. Leaks only grow, and the failure mode of "small leak" is "sudden big leak far from home." **Stop driving:** level dropping fast, temp gauge involved, or the low-coolant light mid-drive. That's the overheating episode's fifteen- minute drill starting NOW — a car driven dry of coolant is an engine obituary. [TECH CONFIRM — bless the tiers]

So: coolant never just leaves — it goes somewhere, and the somewhere is findable. The cardboard maps it, the flashlight finds the crusty trails, the squeeze test reads the hoses, the sweet fog names the heater core, and the pressure test settles the invisible cases. Sealed system, solvable mystery. That closes our cooling trilogy — smoke, heat, and leaks. Next time we change fluids entirely: your car is leaking OIL, and the five gaskets that are almost always to blame.
